title: Attacking ECDSA — Nonce Reuse and Weak RNG

questions.question: In ECDSA, the per-signature nonce k should be:
options: Secret, unique per signature, and (ideally) uniformly random
Public so verifiers can check the signature faster
Constant per key so signatures are reproducible
Random-looking, but reuse is fine if the message changes
questions.explanation: If k is reused, leaked, or guessable, the private key d can often be recovered algebraically.

questions.question: Two ECDSA signatures on different messages have the same r value (over the same curve). What is the most likely explanation?
options: They reused the same nonce k (or produced the same k by accident)
The hash function collided, so r must match
The public key is invalid, so r becomes constant
This is normal; r repeats frequently by design
questions.explanation: For a fixed curve and base point, r is derived from k·G. Same r strongly indicates the same k.

questions.question: Given one ECDSA signature (r, s) on message m, and you learn the nonce k used for that signature, which expression recovers the private key d (mod n)?
options: d ≡ (s·k − z) · r^{-1} (mod n)
d ≡ (z − s) · k^{-1} (mod n)
d ≡ (r − z) · s^{-1} (mod n)
d ≡ (s − r) · z^{-1} (mod n)
questions.explanation: From s·k ≡ z + r·d (mod n), rearrange to r·d ≡ s·k − z and multiply by r^{-1}.

questions.question: Two signatures (r, s1) on m1 and (r, s2) on m2 reused the same nonce. Which formula recovers k (mod n)?
questions.explanation: Subtract the two equations s1·k ≡ z1 + r·d and s2·k ≡ z2 + r·d to eliminate d.

questions.question: Why does drawing k from a small range (e.g., 1..65536) break ECDSA even if k is never reused?
options: An attacker can brute-force k by matching r = (k·G)_x mod n, then recover d
Small k makes SHA-256 weaker, which breaks the message hash
Small k makes r equal to k, so the nonce is directly visible
Small k only breaks performance, not security
questions.explanation: If k is guessable, you can treat it as ‘known nonce’ and compute d using a single modular inverse.

questions.question: Which mitigation specifically targets RNG failures that would otherwise cause nonce reuse in ECDSA?
options: Deterministic nonces (RFC6979-style) derived from (d, H(m))
Using a longer hash function output for z
Encoding signatures in DER instead of raw bytes
Verifying signatures with a larger window size
questions.explanation: RFC6979 replaces ‘random k’ with a deterministic HMAC-based derivation so k won’t repeat due to RNG state reuse.

questions.question: Which validation check is a minimum requirement to prevent obvious malformed-signature cases in ECDSA verification?
options: Reject signatures where r or s are not in the range 1..n-1
Accept any r and s; invalid ones will fail naturally
Only check that r != s
Only check that the message hash z is non-zero
questions.explanation: ECDSA requires 1 ≤ r,s < n. Skipping this can turn edge cases into vulnerabilities or inconsistent behavior across implementations.

questions.question: A system uses RFC6979 deterministic nonces for ECDSA. Which statement is true?
options: It prevents RNG-based nonce reuse, but side-channel leaks of k (or k bits) can still recover d
It makes ECDSA signatures unforgeable even if k is leaked once
It guarantees constant-time signing without extra work
It makes ECDSA equivalent to Ed25519 security-wise
questions.explanation: Deterministic nonces remove one major failure mode (bad randomness), but leaking k (or enough of it) is still fatal.
